items.title: Provably Efficient Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation
items.summary: Concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) unifies a diverse range of problems, including standard reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning, and maximum entropy exploration. Unlike standard RL, CURL generally requires estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures. Consequently, existing methods for CURL either sidestep the exploration problem, are restricted to the tabular setting, or lack computationally efficient policy optimization. To address this, we study CURL in finite-horizon episodic bilinear MDPs, where the transition model admits a low-dimensional representation in known feature spaces. We use the bilinear structure to efficiently estimate occupancy measures via low-dimensional feature expectations, and propose a model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO) framework. We first instantiate OCUPO in the on-policy setting, where each iteration uses independent trajectories to estimate the concave utility policy gradient, and prove an $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-4})$ sample complexity. To improve sample efficiency, we then instantiate OCUPO in the off-policy setting. We propose a novel backward feature regression subroutine that reuses trajectories collected by past policies to estimate the occupancy measure of the current policy. Under suitable technical assumptions on the policy class (satisfied, e.g., by log-linear policies with sufficiently expressive features), we prove that the resulting algorithm achieves an $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity, up to a controllable projection error. We further extend our framework to linear MDPs and show that the resulting off-policy algorithm retains the same sample complexity. In these settings, the dependence on $ε$ matches that for standard RL with linear function approximation. Moreover, our algorithms do not rely on the integral oracle required by prior work.

items.title: Reproducer Synthesis for AI-Reported Bugs in the Linux Kernel
items.summary: Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC. We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a new review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution shows what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.

items.title: A Unified Control Framework for Gradient Inversion Defense in Federated Learning
items.summary: Gradient perturbations are widely recognized as an effective defense against gradient inversion attacks in federated learning, but they are equally known to impair optimization, creating a persistent tension between privacy and utility. In this paper, we show that existing gradient perturbation defenses, despite their different formulations, can be unified under a controlled dynamics framework, providing a cohesive understanding of their optimization behavior and enabling the derivation of universal convergence and safety conditions without relying on case-specific analyses. Leveraging this observation, we propose ``Near Orthogonal Gradient Projection (NODE)'', which injects perturbations only along directions orthogonal to the original gradient so that the defended gradient maintains a fixed cosine similarity with the true gradient. By preserving the first-order descent direction, NODE substantially reduces the optimization cost of strong perturbations while maintaining effective protection against gradient inversion attacks. We theoretically establish convergence guarantees under standard optimization assumptions and further show that, under mild conditions on the gradient distribution, NODE remains effective in preventing inversion attacks. Comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and Chest X-ray, together with a variety of gradient inversion attacks, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an improved privacy--utility trade-off over existing defenses across a broad range of training settings.

items.title: Not all world models can doubt: how training objective and architecture shape epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models
items.summary: World models predict how an environment responds to actions, so that candidate actions can be evaluated before execution. Executed actions, or decisions, taken in this manner are only as reliable as the model's predictive capabilities, and predictions in turn are only reliable within the model's experience. Epistemic uncertainty (EU) is the signal that marks where that experience ends. In this work we offer an extensive empirical study on how training objectives and architectures shape epistemic uncertainty of world models. More precisely, we present a controlled comparison of post-hoc EU (last-layer Laplace and ensembles) between two dominant models of different paradigms: 1) LeWorldModel (LeWM): A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), which predicts the next embedding without a decoder, and 2) DreamerV3: A recurrent state-space model (RSSM), which reconstructs the observation from a recurrent latent state. In ten simulated visual-control environments, we follow a controlled state perturbation of the environment state through every stage of the models up to the final EU estimate. We find that the RSSM attenuates the state perturbation through two mechanisms before it reaches an estimator on the predictor feature. Its recurrent update averages over context, so a change in a single frame reaches the state at a fraction of its size and recovers only as the change persists. Its reconstruction objective weights an entity by the pixels it covers, so a small object can be lost due to the training objective. The JEPA has neither mechanism and passes the change through all stages to the uncertainty. We further show that this translates to gaps in five uncertainty related downstream tasks, from unfamiliar-state detection to uncertainty-penalised planning: the RSSM uncertainty misses deviations that its own posterior registers, whereas the JEPA uncertainty reports what its model sees.

items.title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
items.summary: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.

items.title: Counting Beyond Frames: Codec Motion Tells Frozen Diffusion VLMs How Many
items.summary: Counting how many times something happens is among the simplest questions about a video and among the hardest for video-language models, autoregressive and diffusion alike. The difficulty lies between the frames: a model samples only a few of them, while each repetition unfolds as movement in between. Video codecs already record this movement densely as block displacements, and codec-based video models use it to shape their visual input. We are the first to show that this motion provides direct evidence for the count: a candidate count is a testable motion hypothesis, and unwinding the cycles it implies measures how strongly the observed directions support it. We present CoDiCount, a unified training-free framework that turns this test into a count potential and applies it while a frozen diffusion vision-language model (dVLM) denoises its answer. At every denoising step, structured count messages map each option letter, or each grammar-valid edit of an open integer, to the count it expresses and reweight the model's own probabilities within that set. Consistent gains over the official decoders on MotionBench, TOMATO, and SVCBench demonstrate the broad generalization of CoDiCount across diffusion models, datasets, and diverse counting tasks. With CoDiCount, a 7B dVLM outperforms GPT-5.1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro on MotionBench, surpasses GPT-4o and much larger open models on TOMATO, and matches GPT-5.4 on SVCBench.

items.title: DéjàVu: Plurality Consensus by First Repetition
items.summary: We analyze DéjàVu, a simple protocol for plurality consensus: in each synchronous round, each agent samples one uniformly random agent and adopts the first opinion it observes twice, resetting its memory after every adoption. The rule requires neither frequency counters nor knowledge of the population size or the number of opinions. It relies only on repetition detection, an ability documented in single neurons and reflected in the mere-exposure effect. For a population of $n$ agents with $k$ initial opinions, let $M_0$ be the initial count of the plurality opinion (so $n/M_0 \le k$) and $Δ_0$ its bias, the difference between $M_0$ and the count of the second most popular opinion. We prove that, whenever $Δ_0 = Ω(\sqrt{M_0 \log n})$, DéjàVu reaches consensus on the initial plurality opinion within $O(\sqrt{n/M_0} \log(e M_0 / Δ_0) + \log\log n)$ rounds with high probability. Moreover, we show that, for the same bias regime, DéjàVu is asymptotically never slower than the $h$-majority protocol, collecting its $h$ samples one per round, for every fixed choice of $h$, even one chosen optimally for the initial configuration. There are also initial configurations for which DéjàVu is asymptotically faster for every $h$. The opinion counts alone do not determine the dynamics: each adoption depends on a hidden memory filled over many rounds while the population changed, and agents with older (hence fuller) memories tend to reset sooner, so an advantage held mostly by them can be lost. The few rigorous convergence results we are aware of for such dynamics concern only two opinions. We derive the exact law of the memories given the history of opinions and resets, and track how the plurality opinion's advantage is distributed across memory ages, giving more weight to recently reset agents as they are less likely to reset again soon.

items.title: Joule is FLOP: Optimizing Tensor-Core Kernels Beyond Latency Hiding at the GPU Power Wall
items.summary: For a tensor-core kernel whose average board power stays near the GPU's power cap, runtime is approximately the energy consumed per call divided by that cap. Data movement whose latency is hidden by computation still consumes energy; reducing this traffic can raise the sustained clock and shorten execution even without reducing cycle count. We introduce Joule, a framework that accounts for this energy-frequency coupling in tensor-kernel design and scheduling. Its cost model combines hardware event counts, physical data-path energy costs, and nonlinear voltage scaling across domains to solve for sustained frequency and runtime under a power cap. Combining the model with data-movement lower bounds across memory levels and dies yields a power-aware speed of light (PSoL) that quantifies structural and implementation gaps. This analysis guides wide-tile kernels that use the full tensor memory (TMEM) capacity on B200, with fine-grained asynchronous rotation to overlap accumulator readout with tensor-core computation. It also guides power-aware spatial and temporal tile scheduling that accounts for trade-offs among read sharing, locality, and load balance. Given measured event counts, the model achieves 0.69% mean energy prediction error on B200. Across 60 dense-layer shapes, our GEMM delivers geometric-mean speedups of 4.94%, 6.64%, and 2.12% over exhaustively selected cuBLAS algorithms on B200, H100 NVL, and RTX PRO 6000, respectively. For fused Mega-MoE on eight B200 GPUs, the resulting optimizations improve performance by 2.60% to 5.17% over the upstream DeepGEMM baseline with die-local expert weights. We will open source Joule upon publication.

items.title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
items.summary: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/ρ$, and its yield stress $σ_Y/ρ$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.

items.title: CoordRoute: Coordinated Multi-Model Routing for Maximum Compute-Budget Utility
items.summary: Model routing sends each request to one of several large language models (LLMs) of different sizes. In practice, requests share a fixed compute budget: a spending cap on rented model APIs or the capacity of a private GPU cluster. Most existing routers do not account for the total budget: each decides a request on its own, so per-request optima are not optimal overall. We advocate coordinated routing, which allocates the budget across requests to maximize its utility, their total satisfaction, along a predict-plan-rectify route: predict what each model would give and cost, plan the choice against later requests, and rectify it during generation. Each step faces a challenge: a request's gain from each model is uncertain before generation, later arrivals are unknown when a request must start, and observing answers during generation consumes the budget itself. CoordRoute addresses them with relative demand prediction, which compares candidate models through past requests that lead to the same routing choices; a lookahead solver, which charges each choice for what its compute could earn for later requests; and budget-aware runtime correction, which drops or upgrades in-flight requests at the same price, inspecting answers only when it pays off. On Azure Conversation and BurstGPT traces, CoordRoute improves total satisfaction by 18.72% over the strongest existing router.

items.title: Parallel Memory Management in Goose, C++, and Rust: An Experimental Study of Allocation, Reclamation, and Scaling
items.summary: Compiler-managed memory can reduce allocation and reclamation overhead, but its behavior under parallel workloads remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluates Goose v2026.3 against C++ and Rust implementations, including tree variants with individually allocated nodes and contiguous arenas. We benchmarked worker-local dynamic arrays and binary trees using multiple workers on a workstation with four physical cores and eight logical CPUs. Repeated tree experiments included five construction, traversal, and reclamation rounds. Each main experimental configuration was measured in 15 independent process runs. We measured whole-process execution time, release-operation intervals, and memory usage at synchronized checkpoints. We also examined strong and weak scaling. For depth-20 trees with eight workers, Goose achieved 5.62% and 10.95% lower median execution times than the C++ and Rust arenas, respectively. Its additional process RSS at the LIVE checkpoint was comparable to the arenas and substantially lower than that of individually allocated trees, but its virtual memory size was much larger. Logical reclamation did not always reduce resident memory, and Goose showed lower weak-scaling efficiency than the C++ and Rust arenas. Results for dynamic arrays were mixed. These results indicate that compiler-managed storage can be effective for parallel workloads with predictable object lifetimes. However, execution time alone does not capture its memory and scalability trade-offs.

items.title: Operationalizing Quantum Machine Learning for IoT Network Intrusion Detection
items.summary: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased networked systems' exposure to cyber threats, making Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) essential for securing heterogeneous environments. While Deep Learning (DL) has shown strong performance in traffic analysis, Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has recently gained attention as an alternative approach to learn complex traffic patterns. We assess QML's practical applicability to intrusion detection in heterogeneous IoT scenarios. We present a hybrid quantum-classical NIDS and evaluate it on three recent IoT security datasets, under operationally relevant conditions. Beyond detection accuracy, we compare QML with a classical DL baseline across five operational perspectives: (i) performance under data scarcity, (ii) transferability through cross-domain evaluation, (iii) resilience to temporal constraints, (iv) robustness to quantum non-idealities across multiple noisy backends, and (v) prediction trustworthiness through calibration analysis. Experiments on binary and multiclass misuse detection show that DL generally outperforms QML under ideal and noisy conditions. However, QML remains competitive in data-scarcity and domain-shift scenarios and can outperform the DL baseline under temporal constraints.

items.title: Beyond Autoregression: Diffusion Language Model is All Analog In-Memory Computing Need
items.summary: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) enables energy-efficient language-model inference, but hardware non-idealities perturb matrix--vector multiplications and degrade generation quality. Autoregressive (AR) models are especially vulnerable: each token is committed to the causal context at birth, so perturbation-induced errors cascade. We study diffusion language models (DLMs), which iteratively refine a masked sequence, as an alternative paradigm. Across scale-matched model pairs and open checkpoints, DLMs degrade more gracefully than AR counterparts under persistent weight perturbations. Controlled analyses rule out cross-round noise averaging and support delayed token commitment and progressive context resolution as the mechanism. A larger denoising-step budget further shrinks the clean--noisy gap, a DLM-specific latency--robustness knob. We perform large-scale simulation tests across diverse datasets and models using a noise model calibrated from real silicon measurements. Furthermore, on a 16-chip 28nm eFlash AIMC cluster, hybrid on-board measurements show DLMs tolerate $1.4$--$3\times$ larger weight noise, making diffusion-based generation a promising paradigm for noise-resilient AIMC inference.

items.title: This robot helps you lift objects — by looking at your biceps
items.summary: This robot helps you lift objects — by looking at your biceps rachelg Wed, 05/22/2019 - 10:30 Video May 22 '19 Rachel Gordon CSAIL system can mirror a user's motions and follow nonverbal commands by monitoring arm muscles. We humans are very good at collaboration. For instance, when two people work together to carry a heavy object like a table or a sofa, they tend to instinctively coordinate their motions, constantly recalibrating to make sure their hands are at the same height as the other person's. Our natural ability to make these types of adjustments allows us to collaborate on tasks big and small. But a computer or a robot still can't follow a human's lead with ease. We usually either explicitly program them using machine-speak, or train them to understand our words, à la virtual assistants like Siri or Alexa. In contrast, researchers at MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) recently showed that a smoother robot-human collaboration is possible through a new system they developed, where machines help people lift objects by monitoring their muscle movements. Dubbed RoboRaise, the system involves putting electromyography (EMG) sensors on a user's biceps and triceps to monitor muscle activity. Its algorithms then continuously detect changes to the person's arm level, as well as discrete up-and-down hand gestures the user might make for finer motor control. The team used the system for a series of tasks involving picking up and assembling mock airplane components. In experiments, users worked on these tasks with the robot and were able to control it to within a few inches of the desired heights by lifting and then tensing their arm. It was more accurate when gestures were used, and the robot responded correctly to roughly 70 percent of all gestures. Graduate student Joseph DelPreto says he could imagine people using RoboRaise to help in manufacturing and construction settings, or even as an assistant around the house. "Our approach to lifting objects with a robot aims to be intuitive and similar to how you might lift something with another person — roughly copying each other's motions while inferring helpful adjustments," says DelPreto, lead author on a new paper about the project with MIT Professor and CSAIL Director Daniela Rus. "The key insight is to use nonverbal cues that encode instructions for how to coordinate, for example to lift a little higher or lower. Using muscle signals to communicate almost makes the robot an extension of yourself that you can fluidly control." The project builds off the team's existing system that allows users to instantly correct robot mistakes with brainwaves and hand gestures, now enabling continuous motion in a more collaborative way. "We aim to develop human-robot interaction where the robot adapts to the human, rather than the other way around. This way the robot becomes an intelligent tool for physical work," says Rus. EMG signals can be tricky to work with: They're often very noisy, and it can be difficult to predict exactly how a limb is moving based on muscle activity. Even if you can estimate how a person is moving, how you want the robot itself to respond may be unclear. RoboRaise gets around this by putting the human in control. The team's system uses noninvasive, on-body sensors that detect the firing of neurons as you tense or relax muscles. Using wearables also gets around problems of occlusions or ambient noise, which can complicate tasks involving vision or speech. RoboRaise's algorithm then processes biceps activity to estimate how the person's arm is moving so the robot can roughly mimic it, and the person can slightly tense or relax their arm to move the robot up or down. If a user needs the robot to move farther away from their own position or hold a pose for a while, they can just gesture up or down for finer control; a neural network detects these gestures at any time based on biceps and triceps activity. A new user can start using the system very quickly, with minimal calibration. After putting on the sensors, they just need to tense and relax their arm a few times then lift a light weight to a few heights. The neural network that detects gestures is only trained on data from previous users. The team tested the system with 10 users through a series of three lifting experiments: one where the robot didn't move at all, another where the robot moved in response to their muscles but didn't help lift the object, and a third where the robot and person lifted an object together. When the person had feedback from the robot — when they could see it moving or when they were lifting something together — the achieved height was significantly more accurate compared to having no feedback. The team also tested RoboRaise on assembly tasks, such as lifting a rubber sheet onto a base structure. It was able to successfully lift both rigid and flexible objects onto the bases. RoboRaise was implemented on the team's Baxter humanoid robot, but the team says it could be adapted for any robotic platform. In the future, the team hopes that adding more muscles or different types of sensors to the system will increase the degrees of freedom, with the ultimate goal of doing even more complex tasks. Cues like exertion or fatigue from muscle activity could also help robots provide more intuitive assistance. The team tested one version of the system that uses biceps and triceps levels to tell the robot how stiffly the person is holding their end of the object; together, the human and machine could fluidly drag an object around or rigidly pull it taut. The team will present their work at the International Conference on Robotics and Automation this week in Montreal, Canada. The project was funded in part by The Boeing Company. items.title: Minimizing Optical Circuit Reconfigurations for Concurrent Collectives
items.summary: Optical circuit switches (OCSes) provide high-bandwidth point-to-point circuits in GPU clusters, but each optical port attaches to only one peer at a time, and reconfiguring a connection interrupts transmission. In large-model training, these ports are shared by many communication domains, each running its own collective instance, called a CCL kernel; often, several of these kernels execute the same collective at the same time. Because each step of the collective can reach a different peer, domains advancing through the steps in the same order may require a reconfiguration at every step. We introduce the mega CCL kernel to schedule these kernels jointly. When a collective permits its steps to be reordered, different domains can take different legal steps in the same round, letting consecutive rounds share the same circuits and reducing the number of reconfigurations. Because the kernels are interchangeable, we need not decide the steps of every kernel separately. Instead, in each round we count how many kernels run each pattern, and then use bipartite matching to turn those counts into a concrete schedule for each kernel. We call this the count model, as opposed to the direct formulation that decides each kernel separately, and prove that the two give the same configuration sequences and the same optimum while the count model is substantially easier to solve. On a fully loaded 64-supernode, 64-domain scheduling instance, joint scheduling cuts pairwise-AlltoAll reconfigurations from 62 to 3 and HD AllReduce from 10 to 2. In synthetic training replays parameterized by eight real models, it reduces iteration time by up to about 34%; on a 64-GPU test case, the count model solves over six orders of magnitude faster than the direct formulation.

items.title: High-Throughput GPU Decoding of Quantum Bivariate Bicycle Codes under Circuit-Level Noise
items.summary: Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes reduce the physical-qubit overhead of quantum error correction compared to other codes such as Surface codes, but circuit-level faults create dependencies across measurement rounds that limit decoding throughput. We present a parallel-window GPU decoder that combines reusable fault patterns, compact shared-memory state, and persistent GPU workers using min-sum with Relay-BP recovery. On an RTX 5090, the proposed decoder keeps pace with one syndrome round every 1 $μ$s across all four evaluated codes, up to [[144,12,12]] with 63-144 $μ$s median commit delays. This rate has not been demonstrated in prior circuit-level GPU decoding studies and it provides $120\times$ higher decoding throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding. Checking neighboring detector rounds before accepting a decoding result reduces failure rates by up to 65%. For [[144,12,12]] at $p=0.002$, our proposed decoder achieves $7.58\times 10^{-6}$ failures per round, 36% lower than the published belief propagation (BP) with syndrome flipping (BP-SF) result.

items.title: NEVA: Natural-Language Co-Evolution and Validation of Microarchitectures
items.summary: Recent large language model (LLM)-guided evolutionary approaches have demonstrated the potential to automate microarchitectural design exploration. However, existing approaches primarily evolve C++ simulator code rather than reasoning directly about the microarchitectural designs it represents. As C++ code embodies hardware designs with several layers of abstraction, evolving it directly forces LLMs to reason through implementation details rather than the actual architectural mechanisms, hardware state, and decision rules that define a microarchitectural design. To this end, we propose NEVA, an LLM-guided methodology that generates new microarchitectural policies by extracting, integrating and adapting architectural concepts from published research. NEVA extracts the underlying concepts from prior works into a structured knowledge library, which then guides the evolution of joint natural-language architectural specifications. This approach addresses three key challenges: architectural representation in natural language, validation of candidate designs under hardware constraints, and the coordination of microarchitecture components using diagnostic feedback through co-evolution. We evaluate NEVA across single-core and multicore configurations using SPEC CPU2017/2026, Google, GAP, and XSBench workloads, and compare specification-level evolution against code-level evolution across different search strategies. Under Claude Opus 5.5, NEVA discovers designs achieving up to 4.8% higher held-out single-core performance than the Pythia-Mockingjay baseline. A selected EvoX design achieves improvements of 3.4% and 1.5% under full and restricted memory bandwidth, respectively, although its multicore performance does not differ significantly from the baseline. The EvoX search evaluates 40 candidates over 2.2 days, with approximately $320 in LLM usage at API list prices.

items.title: RePrism: Joint Request and Representation Scheduling for LLM Agent Serving
items.summary: Agentic workflows often invoke large language models multiple times. When the dependencies are visible to the serving system, it can use them to schedule requests and cache reusable content, improving workflow execution efficiency. Prior work has largely focused on ordering requests or managing shared resources under a fixed caching scheme. A reusable prompt that specifies model behavior, however, can have multiple representations. We present RePrism, a serving system that jointly selects which ready request to serve and which eligible representation of its prompt to use. Its goal is to improve throughput and shorten session completion time (SCT). The scheduler ranks pairs of requests and representations by combining each pair's immediate value with an estimate of its future value based on the visible workflow. The resource manager allocates GPU memory to both LoRA adapters and cached key-value states. It also coordinates their admission and eviction as memory pressure changes. We compare RePrism with S-LoRA on a dynamic workload with an arrival rate of 1.8 sessions per second, and it achieves 1.37 times the request throughput and reduces P95 SCT by a factor of 4.10. Under controlled load, RePrism reduces mean time to first token by a factor of 5.26 relative to S-LoRA. On a controlled workload, RePrism's joint scoring achieves 2.7% higher request throughput and 12.3% lower mean SCT than a policy that ranks requests before selecting their representations.

items.title: Mayfly: Lifecycle-Aware High-Bandwidth Flash for Recursive Self-Improvement
items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets an LLM improve its agent system by proposing and evaluating candidate variants across tasks. A generation's sessions grow their KV caches together and release them as they finish, creating a burst followed by a decline. At high concurrency, even the KV of sessions ready to run exceeds the GPU's HBM. Offloading that KV to host DRAM or SSDs adds capacity but leaves ready sessions waiting for HBM space before execution. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) can serve the overflow in place, but excessive reads lengthen decode steps and repeated writes consume flash endurance. Our key insight is that where ready KV is read should follow the burst and its decline: from HBF in place while the burst overflows HBM, as much as each step's bandwidth allows, and from HBM again as the decline frees it. A switch between ready and parked decides only whether a block is read, so its flash copy stays valid, and a session's end, which the orchestrator announces, decides when its private KV dies. We present Mayfly, lifecycle-guided HBF management for RSI. Mayfly bounds per-step HBF reads during overflow and returns KV to HBM as sessions finish and free space. It retains a valid backing copy of each block evicted from HBM to avoid rewrites across state transitions, and forwards session-end signals to the controller to avoid copying dead KV during garbage collection. Experimental results show that, at 128 sessions per generation on four added HBF sites, Mayfly finishes 34% sooner than parking the same KV on HBF and 23% sooner than reading it from HBF whenever HBM is full; its gain over parking grows with concurrency, to 55% at 256 sessions on eight sites. Keeping one flash copy per block and trimming at announced session ends avoid write amplification.

items.title: TimeTravelContainer: A Live Forking Sandbox for Stateful Agent Exploration
items.summary: LLM agents that drive stateful tools (e.g., interactive shells, design environments, simulation engines) frequently need to clone, backtrack, and parallelize live sessions to support exploration. However, cloning a live session today requires serializing the tool's in-memory state to disk or relaunching from scratch, both prohibitively slow for interactive exploration. Existing agent sandboxes based on microVMs or kernel patches either serialize full guest memory to storage or require privileged deployment, limiting use on shared compute farms, personal computers, and other restricted environments. We present TimeTravelContainer (TTC), a rootless container runtime that live-forks an entire running container, including processes, memory, filesystem, and network, with copy-on-write (CoW) semantics. Because the bulk of a tool session's memory is typically read-only after the fork point, clones share it automatically and only diverged pages consume additional memory. TTC requires no kernel modifications, hardware virtualization, or root privileges, and runs on all major platforms including Linux, macOS (Apple Silicon), and Windows (WSL 2), making it deployable as a portable foundation for agent harnesses. We evaluate TTC on two agentic electronic design automation (EDA) flows as representative stateful-tool workloads: MAGE (Innovus) and EvoDRC (KLayout). TTC achieves 84.1$\times$ environment cloning speedup, 31--72% memory reduction, and 1.7--9.4$\times$ end-to-end speedup, demonstrating that live forking removes a scaling barrier for agent-driven exploration of stateful tool environments.

items.title: Cross-Layer Characterization and AI-Assisted Diagnosis of C-to-Rust Performance
items.summary: Migrating C code to Rust can significantly improve software security, but understanding the performance implications of such migrations remains challenging. While Rust is often claimed to match C's performance, runtime safety checks, compiler optimizations, and hardware microarchitecture interact in ways that complicate performance diagnosis. We first conduct a systematic cross-layer characterization of 12 benchmarks comprising C implementations and their Rust counterparts. Our study reveals that runtime safety checks do not necessarily dominate performance overhead, as compiler and microarchitectural optimizations often mitigate their costs. Across 8 of the 12 benchmarks, at least one Rust implementation performs within 10% of its C counterpart or outperforms it. Motivated by these findings, we introduce FerroScope, an AI-assisted performance debugger that integrates source-level analysis, compiler optimization remarks, dynamic instruction traces, and hardware performance counters to diagnose performance differences between C and Rust. FerroScope reproduces our manual findings while providing more precise explanations in several cases, including identifying compiler optimizations inhibited by redundant bounds checks. Guided by these diagnoses, we develop an LLVM compiler pass that hoists redundant bounds checks through guarded loop versioning while preserving Rust's panic behavior. The pass enables downstream compiler optimizations, including loop unrolling and conditional-move conversion, reducing Selection Sort's overhead from 2.95x to 1.00x and improving Merge Sort from 1.43x to 0.91x relative to C. Together, our results demonstrate how cross-layer performance characterization and AI-assisted diagnosis can guide safety-preserving compiler optimizations for efficient C-to-Rust migration.

items.title: Breaking Routing And Inter-device Dependencies in Mixture-of-Experts
items.summary: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale, Expert Parallelism (EP) becomes increasingly important for distributing experts across devices. However, the resulting token dispatch and combine operations can become a major bottleneck during inference. Overlapping these communication phases with computation is constrained by the sequential dependencies of standard MoE architectures. We introduce BRAID-MoE, an architecture that pairs laddered residual connections with early routing to relax these dependencies. Laddered residuals enable each expert combine to be deferred to the following block, while early routing computes the next routing decision from the pre-combine residual, with experts still receiving the updated post-combine hidden state. This creates an extended communication window in which the preceding combine and next dispatch can execute back-to-back on a dedicated communication stream, overlapping attention computation. On Qwen3-shaped MoEs with 0.4B-A0.1B and 2.5B-A0.5B parameters, BRAID closely matches sequential training at matched compute, with validation-loss increases of only 1% and 0.5%, respectively. We further demonstrate that existing MoE checkpoints can be adapted to BRAID with limited additional training, largely recovering their original accuracy. On a converted Qwen3-30B-A3B model, BRAID achieves speedups of up to 1.29$\times$ in prefill and 1.37$\times$ in decode, and at least 1.12$\times$ across diverse workloads and EP configurations on one or two four-H100 nodes. It outperforms competing overlap strategies in all tested settings, with the strongest gains when communication is a major latency bottleneck and its duration approaches the available computation window. These results demonstrate that early routing enables more effective communication-computation overlap in MoE inference at a modest cost in model quality.

items.title: Reliability-aware AI Agent Execution in Collaborative Edge Computing: A World Model Approach
items.summary: Collaborative edge computing supports AI agent applications by distributing execution across heterogeneous user-controlled devices with limited resources. This paper studies reliability-aware AI agent execution under node failures and wireless disruptions. These disruptions can make agent execution state unavailable or inconsistent, forcing recovery or recomputation that consumes the remaining deadline budget. Maintaining recoverable execution states can therefore improve request completion before deadlines. We formulate an online AI agent execution management problem that jointly selects resource allocations, state protection actions, and recovery targets to maximize the expected task success rate subject to resource, compatibility, and deadline constraints. We develop a world model that jointly captures evolving agent workflows and recoverable execution state under candidate management actions, accounting for node reliability, network conditions, and resource availability. The model enables the controller to simulate future execution and recovery trajectories under candidate actions and estimate their effects on execution progress and task completion before deadlines. We then employ world model-based model predictive control (WorldMPC) with Monte Carlo rollouts to jointly optimize resource allocation, state protection, and recovery decisions for long-term reliable agent execution under the dynamic environment. We evaluate the proposed approach on the simulation and real-world testbed using real-world and synthetic datasets. Experimental results show that WorldMPC improves task success rate over baselines in both simulation and real-world testbed.

items.title: Norn: Context-Length-Aware Optimization of Weight and KV Cache Placement for Offloaded LLM Inference
items.summary: Offloading model weights and the key-value (KV) cache to host memory enables large language models (LLMs) to run on a single memory-constrained GPU. As the KV cache grows during decoding, GPU memory requirements and the costs of KV cache transfers and attention computation change. However, existing offloading methods generally use static computation assignments and placements of model weights and the KV cache, preventing them from adapting to these changes and degrading inference performance. We propose Norn, a context-length-aware offloaded LLM inference method. Based on offline profiling, Norn co-optimizes computation assignments and placements at the sublayer level, precomputing multiple execution plans and their switching points. During decoding, Norn switches plans as context length increases, overlapping computation and data transfers without knowing the output length in advance. For prefill, Norn employs operator-major chunked prefill to avoid repeated weight transfers and automatically selects the chunk size. Experiments with Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B on two single-GPU systems show up to a 16.8$\times$ speedup in end-to-end latency over Pipelined Sharding and a 4.2$\times$ speedup over its oracle variant with known input and output lengths.

items.title: Energy and Performance Characterization of UxNBs: Toward AI-Driven Non-Terrestrial Open RAN Control
items.summary: UAV-mounted base stations (UxNBs) can provide ondemand 5G coverage, but their limited onboard energy makes power consumption the main operational constraint. items.title: Machine-Learning-Assisted Hybrid Cooling of a Raspberry Pi 5
items.summary: Thermal management is a critical challenge in compact computing platforms operating under sustained high computational loads. Elevated processor temperatures can lead to thermal throttling, degraded performance, and reduced reliability. This study develops and experimentally evaluates a smart hybrid heat sink that integrates passive thermal energy storage with active cooling for sustained device operation. The proposed design comprises an aluminum cavity containing paraffin wax as a phase change material (PCM) embedded within a copper foam and integrated with an adaptively controlled fan. Fan operation is guided by a Random Forest regression model trained on experimentally measured CPU temperature data to predict future CPU temperatures. The predicted temperature is then used to support the adaptive fan control strategy. The heat sink is mounted directly on the CPU of a Raspberry Pi 5 and experimentally evaluated under an extreme CPU workload of approximately 99 percent CPU utilization. The performance of the proposed hybrid system is compared against two benchmark scenarios: passive cooling using PCM embedded in copper foam and a commercial Raspberry Pi 5 active cooler. The proposed heat sink demonstrates superior thermal performance to both benchmarks, achieving peak CPU temperature reductions of approximately 9 C relative to the PCM-copper foam configuration and 6 C relative to the commercial active cooler.

items.title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes
items.summary: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement. Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.

items.title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
items.summary: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.

items.title: Estimating GPU Roofline Arithmetic Intensity with Off-the-Shelf LLMs and Compiler Artifacts
items.summary: GPU developers use profiling to understand computation and data movement, but access to target hardware can delay optimization. We investigate whether off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) can estimate Roofline arithmetic intensity (the ratio of floating-point operations (FLOPs) to device-memory bytes) without executing the target GPU workload. We evaluate three models (deepseek-v4-flash, gemini-3.7-flash, and gpt-5.6-sol) across 179 combinations of five kernel families, four NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, four parallel runtimes (CUDA, HIP, OpenMP, and OpenCL), and modified code variants, comparing source-only queries, queries with compiler artifacts, and sandboxed agentic analysis. Compiler artifacts raise the share of arithmetic-intensity estimates within a factor of 1.20 of profiled values from 8-14% to 26-32%, while the resulting bandwidth-bound or compute-bound classifications are correct in 78-92% of runs. With compiler artifacts, FLOP estimates meet the 1.20x tolerance in 59-88% of runs, compared with 36-40% for device-memory traffic. Agentic analysis increases the share of arithmetic-intensity estimates within the 1.20x tolerance by 6.5 percentage points for gpt-5.6-sol, at 3.6x the median cost and 2.5x the median latency of compiler-assisted queries; the other models incur higher costs without a statistically clear improvement. These findings suggest LLM estimates could help prioritize optimization when GPU access is constrained, while identifying cache-dependent device-memory traffic as the main obstacle to precise arithmetic-intensity prediction.

items.title: Scalable Placement for Disaggregated LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Fleets
items.summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) at the edge is increasingly desirable for privacy-sensitive applications and scenarios that require data to remain on local devices. However, edge environments are constrained by limited computational resources and exhibit substantial device heterogeneity, making efficient LLM serving challenging. These limitations become particularly pronounced under bursty demand, where congestion and queue buildup can significantly increase response latency. Replicating the model into multiple pipeline instances can improve serving capacity and reduce congestion. Yet, deciding how devices should be grouped into replicas, assigning replicas to prefill or decode functions, and partitioning model layers across heterogeneous devices jointly creates a large combinatorial optimization problem. We present Spade, a scalable and runtime-efficient placement planner for disaggregated LLM serving with pipeline replication across heterogeneous edge clusters. Spade introduces a dominance-based pruning technique that discards inferior replica candidates and recursively eliminates larger candidates that contain them, dramatically shrinking the search space. It further combines a water-filling approach for layer partitioning with a bounded multidimensional knapsack formulation that optimizes placement under a congestion-aware objective. On a synthetic fleet of 30 devices spanning five hardware classes, Spade finds the optimal placement in 441ms. In contrast, a genetic-search baseline augmented with dynamic-programming partitioning requires approximately two hours and still produces solutions with a 19.7% worse congestion objective. When evaluated on fleets containing ten device types, Spade's pruning strategy eliminates 99.6% of candidate placements while yielding the same surviving candidate set as exhaustive enumeration.

items.title: Leveraging Persistent Field-of-View and Multipath Segment Routing for Traffic Engineering in LEO Satellite Constellations
items.summary: The emergence of low earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations poses fundamental challenges for traditional rout- ing paradigms due to high node mobility, frequent topology changes, and constrained on-board resources. This paper pro- poses a segment routing (SR) framework that offloads route computation and control signaling from resource-constrained LEO switches to more powerful medium earth orbit (MEO) con- trollers. We first establish sufficient conditions for the persistence of user-to-satellite and LEO-to-MEO field-of-view (FoV) con- nectivity throughout a virtual topology (VT) snapshot interval, enabling handover-free operation. Leveraging this persistence, we formulate the MEO control domain partitioning problem as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) to minimize control over- head while assigning disjoint segment routing domains (SRDs) to MEO controllers. Within each SRD, we develop a multipath SR- based traffic engineering (SR-TE) formulation that splits traffic among four minimum-hop-count path types to minimize maxi- mum link utilization. We solve this linear program (LP) using a distributed primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) approach that preserves SRD-level privacy and requires only AllReduce communication. Simulations on the Starlink/GPS combination demonstrate our approach reduces maximum link utilization by more than 13.09%, 11.84%, and 12.50%, respectively, com- pared to traditional minimum hop count routing (MHCR) and traffic-oblivious load-balancing methods for Starlink, Kuiper, and OneWeb.

items.title: Embodied Intelligence for Spectrum Map Construction in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks
items.summary: Accurate spectrum map construction by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is crucial for intelligent resource management in low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs). Although various construction approaches have been investigated, their performance often degrades under extremely sparse sampling because purely data-driven models may not capture the underlying propagation physics. To address these challenges, an embodied intelligence framework is proposed, which synergistically integrates closed-loop perception-cognition-execution (PCE) coupling and embodied exploration to achieve precise and efficient spectrum construction. Based on this framework, a corresponding embodied cognition and decision network (ECDNet) with three tightly coupled modules is designed. Specifically, by leveraging distance-aware convolutions, the semantic bridge, and adaptive feature alignment mechanisms, ECDNet establishes the bidirectional information flow between construction and decision-making. Simulation results show that ECDNet achieves a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.787 dBm at 4.00% sampling under the non-revisiting spiral protocol. Furthermore, a practical UAV-based spectrum construction platform is developed and field-deployed to provide prototype-level evidence that the sensing, cognition, and action modules execute as a closed loop on size, weight, and power constrained UAV edge devices.

items.title: FlashQLA: Efficient Context Parallelism for Gated DeltaNet
items.summary: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. items.title: Analysis of Federated Graph Neural Networks for Predicting Nuclear Core Properties
items.summary: Federated learning has grown in popularity owing to the increasing data privacy and safety concerns. It allows multiple parties to collaboratively train a model without exchanging their raw data. As an example of highly sensitive infrastructure of national importance, nuclear reactors benefit from this approach, where---while pooling multiple large datasets from different institutions could improve machine learning solutions---the confidentiality of the datasets is paramount. In this paper, we demonstrate that a graph neural network (GNN) outperforms the convolutional neural network (CNN) baseline in a federated setting for a use case concerning nuclear reactor core optimization. The GNN architecture is better suited for the nuclear reactor geometry as, unlike the CNN, it does not require padding the cylindrical core and does not assume translation invariance. The key finding of this work is that input representation is more important than model size and complexity. More sophisticated federated algorithms were employed, but the improvements derived were of lower magnitude. Experimenting with training corpus volume led to the discovery that greater fuel inventory variance is more beneficial than arrangements of existing cases, which is a direct consequence of data heterogeneity. Going forward, focus will remain on enhancing the input and readout representation.

items.title: On the Design of a Slow Control Interlock System for the European GateMate FPGA
items.summary: Slow Control Systems (SCSs) are essential for the monitoring, configuration, and protection of distributed safety-critical systems in scientific, industrial, and medical applications. Although software-based SCS architectures offer flexibility and scalability, they suffer from software aging and non-deterministic latencies, which limit long-term reliability and timely reaction to critical errors, often requiring additional hardware interlock systems. This paper presents an FPGA-centric lightweight Slow Control Interlock System (SCIS) designed to achieve deterministic ultra-low-latency reaction times in long-running dependable systems. System parameters are acquired and fused at runtime in a Supervisory Monitor Unit (SMU), enabling real-time fault condition classification and prioritization through configurable priority rules and triggering kill-switch actions with microsecond-scale latency. The proposed SMU has been described in VHDL as vendor-agnostic architecture, and assessed on the 28-nm GateMate M1A1 FPGA, using the open-source OSS-CAD-Suite toolchain. Experimental results show that the SMU architecture utilizes only 37,6% of LUTs, 9,4% of FFs, and 35,9% of BRAM. Furthermore, this low resource utilization allow to achieve 40,48 ms reconfiguration time, using OSS-CAD-Suite including gmpack v1.13. This is a key metric for rejuvenation and consequently for enabling aging mitigation in critical applications. Offloading the Ethernet stack to the W5500 Ethernet module and integrating the Grafana dashboard provides a lightweight, deterministic SCIS. This demonstrates the feasibility of our FPGA-centric architecture as a solution to the problem of combining ultra-low-latency interlock capabilities with the scalability of software-based systems.

items.title: WorldExpand: Building Coherent 3D Worlds via Sparse Joint Panoramic Expansion
items.summary: Constructing complete 3D worlds from a single panorama is challenging because large portions of the scene remain unobserved. Existing panoramic-video methods expand spatial coverage through dense sequential generation, but neighboring frames contain substantial redundancy, long trajectories accumulate errors, and independently generated directions may be inconsistent. We present WorldExpand, which formulates single-panorama world expansion as the generation of sparse, complementary, and high-resolution panoramic observations. This representation concentrates the generation budget on informative scene regions and preserves the fine-grained details required for 3D construction. WorldExpand addresses two key challenges: where to observe and how to synthesize. Our Coverage-Guided View Selection identifies informative target locations using scene-adaptive quadrants and warp-based coverage scores, while our Joint Panoramic Diffusion uses Gaussian-splatting-based geometric warps to jointly synthesize four pose-grounded and cross-view-consistent panoramas. A diagnostic-guided global--local attention schedule retains global attention only in sensitive layers, reducing the training and inference costs of high-resolution joint generation. The resulting posed panoramas can be directly fed into an existing reconstruction pipeline to build an explicit 3D representation. Experiments show that WorldExpand recovers content behind occluders and around distant corners, improves both novel-view synthesis and downstream 3D reconstruction metrics across various datasets, and generalizes robustly to diverse in-the-wild scenes. WorldExpand runs significantly faster than the state-of-the-art panoramic-video method while producing higher-resolution observations with stronger cross-view consistency.

items.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
items.summary: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

items.title: Beyond Feature Fusion: Sensor-Grounded Semantic-Spiking Learning for Robust Object Detection
items.summary: Underexposure weakens object details, and overexposure obscures boundaries. Spike cameras encode light into high-frequency binary streams. Long-window spike counts give stable appearance cues, while short observations reveal changes in firing rates from sparse measurements. We propose SPIRE, a sensor-grounded semantic-spiking framework for illumination-robust object detection from a single spike stream. SPIRE builds an appearance view from the full packet through detection-oriented illumination adaptation and constructs a sequence of cumulative views from progressively longer prefixes. Each prefix supplies a rate map, an edge map, and a rate difference that tracks changes as spikes accumulate. At selected scales, ANN features and spike-derived initialization jointly set the initial membrane potentials and firing thresholds, allowing semantic cues to shape the responses during temporal encoding. Local spike-count contrasts supervise both branches during training. items.title: WADJET: Whole-Job Authorization and Dispatch for Job Execution Trust on FPGA System-on-Chip Accelerators
items.summary: On an FPGA system-on-chip, the software that submits work to an accelerator also decides what the accelerator does. It writes the registers one by one, and the hardware runs whatever it finds, so faulty or compromised software can change one address or resend a job. Existing protections decide who may reach an accelerator or keep its data safe. Deciding whether one job was approved and is still unused takes three things in one place: the only way to the accelerator, the whole job held back until checked, and a record of used approvals. WADJET puts the three in one gate in FPGA logic. A separate authority encrypts and authenticates each approved job, with a sequence number, using Ascon-AEAD128. The gate verifies the whole job before releasing any part, accepts only a newer sequence number, uses it up, and writes the registers of an unmodified accelerator itself. The gate replaces only the processor's direct line to the registers and works beside the existing protections. In a software model, a check on each write ran jobs mixed from two approved ones; the whole-job rule released none. Its release path is proven on the Verilog for all inputs. On a Zynq-7020 running a language model, it released all 21,000 approved jobs and none of 14,700 altered or repeated ones. It needs a third of the lookup tables of ShEF's register protection, which protects more, and adds about ten microseconds to starting a job. It assumes trusted control of its key, reset, and configuration.

items.title: Anytime-Valid Sequential Verification for Sensing-Efficient Robot Navigation under Perception Uncertainty
items.summary: When a robot navigates an unfamiliar grid, noisy sensor readings can make it hard to tell whether the cells along its next move are free. Additional scans can reduce that uncertainty, but a fixed scan count spends the same sensing effort at every position. In a static-grid simulation, a sequential rule uses a Gaussian likelihood ratio to determine when the cells newly covered by the robot's footprint have enough evidence of free space. On 324 held-out scenarios from 18 public maps, the sequential gate and a four-scan reference chosen on validation data both completed every mission without an observed collision. With their respective validation-selected routing weights, the gate averaged 123.15 scans per episode versus 224.13 for the reference, a reduction of 45.05% (95% map-stratified bootstrap interval: 42.21--48.95%). In a retrospective check on the same scenarios with routing weights held equal, the reductions were 43.91% and 43.37% at the two tested weights, with all missions completed. On 216 scenarios from 12 previously unused maps, allocating more of the same certification error budget near the initial start--goal rectangle cut the sequential gate's scan count by a further 11.58%. The spatial variant completed 206 missions versus 208 for the original gate and increased computation time. The collision bound depends on the assumed observation model and footprint geometry. In a stress test with persistent per-cell bias, the original gate completed 0 of 54 missions.

items.title: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence
items.summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.

items.title: MERLoc: Robust Robot Localization in Dynamic Environments with Pose-Based Retrieval over 3D Gaussian Splatting References
items.summary: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.

items.title: Autonomous Ergodic Robotic Palpation for Elastic Mapping of Curved Soft Tissues
items.summary: Autonomous robotic palpation offers repeatable, quantitative estimates of tissue properties for stiff inclusion localization. However, existing methods often rely on prior mesh models or planar surface assumptions that do not generalize to complex human anatomy. We propose an ergodic palpation framework that operates directly on curved soft surfaces using point cloud data. Central to our approach is the Laplace--Beltrami operator, which grounds both online estimation and exploration in the surface intrinsic geometry. We estimate local viscoelastic parameters using an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) and fuse them into a surface-aware Gaussian Process (GP). This probabilistic model drives a diffusion-based ergodic motion planner, generating a continuous exploration trajectory that feeds the new informative samples back to the GP in a closed loop. Throughout this process, a hybrid force-impedance controller regulates interaction forces to maintain contact. We evaluate the approach against existing methods in simulation and validate it in physical experiments on tissue-mimicking silicone phantoms with varying geometries and viscoelastic properties, demonstrating geometry-consistent mapping and stiff inclusion localization under contact-rich conditions.

items.title: A Local-Counting Approach for Distributed Induced Path Detection
items.summary: A well-known application of the celebrated color-coding technique is fast detection of paths in a distributed setting with limited bandwidth, by propagating a signal along colorful paths [Even et al., DISC 2017]. However, since vertices of the same color are indistinguishable by this procedure, it cannot detect induced paths, as they appear the same as cycles. We make the following observation. If, for a given edge, we \emph{count} the number of such signals over all permutations of the random coloring that terminate at that edge, then we can separate an induced path from a cycle: an induced path contributes one to that count, while a cycle contributes two. Refining and generalizing this observation gives our \emph{local-counting approach}, which allows us to separate induced paths from any other subgraph. We establish the following end results, all improving upon the state of the art in their round complexities and refined detection variants. * An $O(1)$-round algorithm for induced $P_4$ detection. * $O(Δ)$-round algorithms for detection of induced $P_5$ and $P_6$. * An $\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})$-round algorithm for detection of induced $P_5$ in induced-$C_4$ free graphs.

items.title: Scaling Architectural Simulation to Giga Instructions Per Second
items.summary: The cost of detailed architectural simulation constrains design-space exploration, while parallelization across simulated cores offers limited host concurrency for single-core and small multicore targets. We present GIPSim, an instruction-driven simulator that derives instruction timing from dependencies and resource constraints, reducing the overhead of updating pipeline state every simulated cycle. It applies synchronization-guided temporal decomposition to recorded execution, exposing host parallelism beyond the target core count. GIPSim replays the resulting segments in parallel and aggregates their durations through a dependency graph to estimate overall execution time, with replay contexts reconstructed using retained microarchitectural state, warmup, and synchronization-guided cache eviction. This accounts for synchronization waits without requiring host workers to follow target execution order. We evaluate GIPSim using QEMU traces of application and operating system execution on multi-core x86-64, AArch64, and RV64GC systems. GIPSim achieves an average single-node simulation throughput of 13.8 million instructions per second (MIPS) with one worker and 1{,}010 MIPS with 96 workers, peaking at 1{,}421 MIPS. The corresponding mean absolute percentage errors in execution cycles relative to gem5 are 7.52\% and 7.43\%, respectively.

items.summary: Blockchain in conjunction with the Internet of Things (IoT) is changing the management of spatiotemporal data in a way that has never been possible before now. items.title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
items.summary: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

items.title: SceneDesigner3D: Agentic Evolutionary Search for Principled Rearrangement of 3D Indoor Scenes
items.summary: Scene rearrangement is an essential task for 3D content creation applications, requiring generation of diverse, aesthetic and functional scene rearrangements. We present SceneDesigner3D, an agentic evolutionary search method for 3D indoor scene rearrangement that systematically explores the design space of 3D scenes and generates multiple solutions according to common interior design principles. Given an input scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D represents the rearrangement as an editable program and evolves a population of candidate layouts. Starting from distinct design ideas, a VLM agent mutates the programs by refining promising candidates, exploring new rearrangement strategies or redesigning from scratch, while verifying the layouts for physical validity. Proposals are scored by a VLM judge for adherence to the input prompt and satisfaction of design principles such as balance, zoning and emphasis, as well as numerically computed principles such as circulation and clutter. An archive of top-performing, structurally varied candidates further increases diversity of rearrangements. Experiments on the SAGE-10k and SceneSmith datasets show that SceneDesigner3D improves prompt adherence and computed design principle scores over baselines by up to 5.1% and 15.2%, respectively.
